facts.statement: The genus Kunpengopterus was named and described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2010.
facts.quote: Kunpengopterus was named and described by Wang Xiaolin, Alexander Wilhelm Armin Kellner, Jiang Shunxing, Cheng Xin, Meng Xi and Taissa Rodrigues in 2010.

facts.statement: The generic name Kunpengopterus combines a Chinese mythological fish-whale and a Greek word for wing.
facts.quote: The generic name combines the Kun, a large fish or whale from Chinese folklore that could transform itself into the Peng, a gigantic colourful bird providing a mythological explanation of the northern lights, with a Latinised Greek pteron, "wing".

facts.statement: A second species, Kunpengopterus antipollicatus, was described by Xuanyu Zhou and colleagues in 2021.
facts.quote: A second species of Kunpengopterus was described in 2021 by Xuanyu Zhou and colleagues, Kunpengopterus antipollicatus.

facts.statement: The specific name antipollicatus refers to an opposable thumb on the wing.
facts.quote: The specific name is from the Ancient Greek anti "opposite" and pollex "thumb", and refers to the opposed first finger (a thumb) on the wing.

facts.statement: The type species Kunpengopterus sinensis had an elongated head measuring 10.7 cm in length.
facts.quote: Kunpengopterus sinensis has an elongated head, 10.7 cm long.

facts.statement: A low bony crest behind the eyes was elongated by cartilage and possibly extended to the back by a skin flap.
facts.quote: A low bony crest is present on the skull, just behind the eyes; preserved soft tissue shows it was elongated by cartilage and a yellow discolouration indicates it was perhaps enlarged to the back by a skin flap.

facts.statement: Kunpengopterus possessed a long, stiff tail.
facts.quote: Kunpengopterus has a long stiff tail.

facts.statement: The fifth toe of Kunpengopterus was long and strongly curved.
facts.quote: The fifth toe is also long and strongly curved.

facts.statement: Kunpengopterus antipollicatus had an opposable thumb, a feature rare among non-mammals.
facts.quote: K. antipollicatus has an opposable pollux or thumb, which is rare amongst non-mammals.

facts.statement: Kunpengopterus antipollicatus was nicknamed "Monkeydactyl" due to its thumbs.
facts.quote: K. antipollicatus has also been called the "Monkeydactyl", because of the thumbs.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence includes preserved soft parts and remains of a possibly regurgitated fish.
facts.quote: Aside from the bones some soft parts were also preserved and the remains of a possibly regurgitated fish.

facts.statement: Kunpengopterus lived during the middle to late Jurassic in northeastern China.
facts.quote: Kunpengopterus is a genus of wukongopterid pterosaur from the middle-late Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation of northeastern China.

facts.statement: The genus lived between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Kimmeridgian (168.2 to 152.21 million years ago)

facts.statement: Kunpengopterus is classified within the family Wukongopteridae.
facts.quote: Kunpengopterus was assigned to the Wukongopteridae, a family of pterosaurs showing a mix of basal and derived pterodactyloid traits.

facts.statement: The type species is known from an almost complete skeleton found in the Tiaojishan Formation in western Liaoning.
facts.quote: K. sinensis is known from the holotype specimen IVPP V16047, an almost complete skeleton with complete skull and lower jaws recovered from rocks of the Tiaojishan Formation in Linglongta, Jianchang County, western Liaoning.

facts.statement: An additional specimen with a skull was referred to the genus in 2017.
facts.quote: In 2017, an additional specimen, IVPP V 23674, was referred and described. It consists of a skeleton with skull.

facts.statement: A specimen nicknamed "Mrs T" was preserved with an egg impression between its thighs.
facts.quote: This specimen was preserved with the impression of an egg between its thighs in close association with its pelvis.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the egg-bearing specimen represents sexual dimorphism, as researchers suggest crest size may vary with age rather than sex.
facts.quote: However, this hypothesis has been criticized. Pterosaur researcher Kevin Padian questioned some of the conclusions drawn by Lü et al., suggesting in a 2011 interview that, in other animals with elaborate display crests (such as ceratopsian dinosaurs), the size and shape of the crests change dramatically with age.

facts.statement: Kunpengopterus laid eggs with a parchment-like, soft shell.
facts.quote: The eggs of Kunpengopterus had a parchment-like, soft shell.

facts.statement: The eggs were small relative to the mother's size, resembling modern reptiles more than birds.
facts.quote: The eggs were small compared to the size of the mother (the "Mrs T" specimen weighed between 110 g and 220 g), also more like modern reptiles than birds.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Kunpengopterus likely buried many small eggs and that juveniles could fly immediately after hatching.
facts.quote: David Unwin, a co-author of the paper, suggested that Kunpengopterus probably laid many small eggs at a time and buried them, and that juveniles could fly upon hatching, requiring little to no parental care.

facts.statement: Analysis of a counterplate suggests the animal had two active ovaries producing one egg at a time.
facts.quote: However, in 2015, the counterplate of the specimen was reported, IVPP V18403, which showed a single additional egg present in the body, indicating that there were two active ovaries, producing a single egg at a time.
